newsitem.title: Italy: Italy banks in "historic" restructuring deal.
newsitem.headline: Italy banks in "historic" restructuring deal.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government on Thursday heralded a preliminary agreement between banking association ABI and unions over job cuts and restructuring in the banking sector as a historic deal.

The accord, which was struck late on Wednesday, gives unions and management 60 days to finalise plans for a comprehensive overhaul of the sector, which financial analysts say is heavily overstaffed by comparison with other European countries.

"This is a deal unheard of in the economic history of our country," cabinet secretary Enrico Micheli told a news conference. "For the first time the banking sector has to face up to a true and proper restructuring to get up to date."
Bank of Italy Governor Antonio Fazio praised the deal.
"It's headed in the direction we hoped for," he told reporters. "We'll have to see how it is put into practice."

Micheli said labour costs at Italian banks were around 30 percent higher than the European average and added that the sector needed to shed between 30,000-45,000 jobs, around a tenth of the total workforce.

Wednesday's government-brokered accord, reached after more than 10 hours of talks between the various parties, foresees the creation of a national fund which is expected to help finance eventual lay-offs in the sector.
Banks will be asked to give the fund a sum equivalent to 0.5 percent of their total salary bill.
Unions and management also signalled the need for greater flexibility over contracts and schemes to help workers directly invest in their banks.

Micheli and Labour Minister Tiziano Treu mediated Wednesday's marathon session. Unions and management will now work together on the fine print and the government has pledged to review the situation on July 10. "The meeting with unions will continue in an orderly fashion and will centre on labour costs, job flexibility and contract rigidity," said Maurizio Sella, who led Abi's negotiating team.
The cabinet secretary said the reform had to achieve concrete results within four years and said the government would review the impact of the accord in one year's time.
Banking analysts have warned that overstaffing in Italian banks must be addressed and swift restructuring implemented if the sector is to achieve the sort of profitability seen elsewhere in Europe.
However the issue is deeply controversial in a country where it is extremely difficult to fire people who are on full-time contracts.
Earlier this week staff at Italy's Banca di Roma staged a one-day strike to protest against plans to cut the bank's 22,000-strong workforce by more than 4,000 people.

Analysts argue that such downscaling is vital if Italian banks are to boost their feeble return-on-equity, which in 1995 struggled to an average 2.15 percent against around 20 percent from their leaner British competitors.
Employee costs in the sector rose 6.8 percent in 1996 while inflation grew by just 3.9 percent.
